stem: Ali walks 30 m due east and then 40 m due north. The magnitude of his displacement is
explanation: Displacement is the straight line from start to finish, the hypotenuse of a right triangle: √(30² + 40²) = √2500 = 50 m. 70 m is the total distance walked, not the displacement, and 2500 m forgets to take the square root.

stem: Hamza runs exactly one lap of a circular track of radius 50 m in 40 s. The magnitude of his average velocity for the lap is
explanation: After one full lap he is back at the starting point, so his displacement is zero and average velocity = displacement/time = 0. The value 2.5π m/s (2π × 50/40) is his average speed, which uses the distance travelled, not the displacement.

stem: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
explanation: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Speed and distance are only magnitudes (scalars), and time has no direction at all.

stem: A bus travels from Islamabad to a town 60 km away at a steady 30 km/h and returns along the same road at a steady 60 km/h. Its average speed for the whole trip is
explanation: Total distance = 120 km; total time = 60/30 + 60/60 = 2 h + 1 h = 3 h, so average speed = 120/3 = 40 km/h. 45 km/h is the simple mean of the two speeds, which is wrong because the bus spends more time at the lower speed.

stem: The position of a particle moving along the x-axis is x = 4t² − 2t, where x is in metres and t in seconds. Its velocity at t = 3 s is
explanation: Velocity is v = dx/dt = 8t − 2, so at t = 3 s, v = 24 − 2 = 22 m/s. 30 m/s is the position value x(3) = 36 − 6, read wrongly as velocity, and 24 m/s forgets the −2 term.

stem: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of
explanation: Acceleration a = Δv/Δt, the rate of change of velocity with time. The rate of change of displacement with time is velocity, not acceleration.

stem: A car starts from rest and moves with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s². Its velocity after 5 s is
explanation: Using vf = vi + at = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 m/s. 5 m/s is the average velocity over the 5 s, not the final velocity, and 7 m/s wrongly adds a and t.

stem: A motorcycle starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 4 m/s². The distance it covers in the first 6 s is
explanation: s = vit + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 4 × 36 = 72 m. 144 m forgets the factor ½, and 24 m is the final velocity (at = 24 m/s), not a distance.

stem: A train moving at 20 m/s applies its brakes and comes to rest with uniform deceleration after travelling 100 m. The magnitude of its deceleration is
explanation: vf² = vi² − 2as gives 0 = 400 − 2a × 100, so a = 400/200 = 2 m/s². 4 m/s² comes from dividing 400 by 100 and forgetting the factor 2 in 2as.

stem: A stone dropped from rest from the top of a tower reaches the ground in 4 s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, the height of the tower is
explanation: h = ½gt² = ½ × 10 × 16 = 80 m. 160 m forgets the factor ½, and 40 m is the final speed (gt = 40 m/s) mistaken for a height.

stem: Usman throws a ball vertically upward with a speed of 30 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, the ball returns to the point of projection after
explanation: Time to reach the top is u/g = 30/10 = 3 s, and the fall back takes the same time, so total time = 2u/g = 6 s. 3 s is only the time of ascent.

stem: A car starts from rest and moves with a uniform acceleration of 4 m/s². The distance it covers during the 5th second of its motion is
explanation: Distance in the 5th second = s(5) − s(4) = ½ × 4 × (25 − 16) = 2 × 9 = 18 m. 50 m is the total distance in the first 5 s, and 32 m is the total in the first 4 s.

stem: A body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration. It covers 10 m in the first 2 s. The distance it covers in the next 2 s is
explanation: From rest, s ∝ t², so in 4 s it covers 10 × (4/2)² = 40 m. The distance in the next 2 s is 40 − 10 = 30 m (the 1 : 3 ratio for equal successive intervals). 40 m is the total in 4 s, not the distance in the second interval.

stem: A car at rest at a traffic light starts with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s² just as a truck moving at a constant 10 m/s passes it in the same direction. The car catches the truck at a distance from the light of
explanation: They meet when ½ × 2 × t² = 10t, giving t = 10 s, and the distance is 10 × 10 = 100 m. 25 m is where the car is at t = 5 s, when the two speeds are equal and the gap is largest, not where they meet.

stem: The velocity of a car increases uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. The distance it travels in this time is
explanation: For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (10 + 30)/2 = 20 m/s, so distance = 20 × 5 = 100 m. 150 m wrongly uses the final speed for the whole 5 s, and 50 m uses only the initial speed.

stem: The SI unit of acceleration is
explanation: Acceleration = change in velocity (m s⁻¹) divided by time (s), giving m s⁻². m s⁻¹ is the unit of velocity and kg m s⁻¹ is the unit of momentum.

stem: A stone is dropped from rest and falls freely through 45 m. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, its speed just before it hits the ground is
explanation: vf² = 2gh = 2 × 10 × 45 = 900, so vf = 30 m/s. √450 m/s forgets the factor 2, and 900 m/s forgets to take the square root.

stem: For a body moving with constant velocity, its acceleration is
explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; if velocity does not change in magnitude or direction, the acceleration is zero. A constant velocity does not mean a constant non-zero acceleration.

stem: A car moving at 30 m/s brakes with a uniform deceleration of 5 m/s² until it stops. The distance it covers in the last one second before stopping is
explanation: The last second of a uniform deceleration to rest mirrors the first second of a uniform acceleration from rest: s = ½ × 5 × 1² = 2.5 m. 90 m is the total stopping distance (30²/(2 × 5)), and 5 m uses a × t without the ½.

stem: Bilal cycles in a straight line at 8 m/s for 6 s and then at 2 m/s for 12 s in the same direction. His average velocity for the whole motion is
explanation: Total displacement = 8 × 6 + 2 × 12 = 48 + 24 = 72 m in a total time of 18 s, so average velocity = 72/18 = 4 m/s. 5 m/s is the simple mean of the two speeds, which ignores that the times are unequal.

stem: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m/s from the edge of a roof 25 m above the ground and falls to the ground beside the building. Taking g = 10 m/s², the time it takes to reach the ground is
explanation: Taking up as positive, −25 = 20t − 5t², so t² − 4t − 5 = 0 and (t − 5)(t + 1) = 0, giving t = 5 s. 4 s is only the time to return to roof level (2u/g), and 2 s is the time to the highest point.

stem: A body is dropped from rest and falls freely. The distances it covers in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds of its fall are in the ratio
explanation: Total distances after 1, 2, 3 s are in the ratio 1 : 4 : 9 (s ∝ t²), so the distances in each separate second are 1, 4 − 1 = 3 and 9 − 4 = 5. The ratio 1 : 4 : 9 is for total distances, not for each second.

stem: A balloon is rising vertically at a steady 10 m/s. When it is 40 m above the ground, a stone is released from it. Taking g = 10 m/s², the stone reaches the ground after
explanation: The stone starts with the balloon's velocity, 10 m/s upward. Taking up as positive, −40 = 10t − 5t², so t² − 2t − 8 = 0 and (t − 4)(t + 2) = 0, giving t = 4 s. 2√2 s wrongly treats the stone as dropped from rest (40 = 5t²).

stem: A cyclist moving at 5 m/s accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 4 s. The distance covered in these 4 s is
explanation: s = vit + ½at² = 5 × 4 + ½ × 2 × 16 = 20 + 16 = 36 m. 52 m forgets the ½ (20 + 32), while 16 m and 20 m each use only one of the two terms.

stem: Which pair consists of two scalar quantities?
explanation: Speed and distance both have magnitude only, so both are scalars. Each of the other pairs contains a vector: velocity, displacement and force all have direction.

stem: The slope of a velocity-time graph gives the
explanation: Slope = Δv/Δt, which is the definition of acceleration. Displacement is given by the area under the velocity-time graph, not its slope.

stem: The area between a velocity-time graph and the time axis represents the
explanation: Area = velocity × time, which has the dimensions of displacement, so the area under a velocity-time graph gives the displacement. Acceleration is the slope of the graph, not the area.

stem: The velocity-time graph of a body is a straight line parallel to the time axis, above the axis. The body is moving with
explanation: A horizontal line means the velocity has the same non-zero value at every instant, so the velocity is uniform and the slope (acceleration) is zero. Uniform acceleration would need a sloping straight line.

stem: The velocity-time graph of a car is a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 20 m/s at t = 4 s. The distance covered by the car in these 4 s is
explanation: The distance is the area of the triangle under the graph: ½ × 4 × 20 = 40 m. 80 m forgets the ½ of the triangle, and 5 m is the slope (the acceleration in m/s²), not a distance.

stem: A velocity-time graph shows a van speeding up uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 3 s, moving at a constant 12 m/s for the next 4 s and then slowing uniformly to rest in a further 2 s. The total distance covered is
explanation: Area = ½ × 3 × 12 + 4 × 12 + ½ × 2 × 12 = 18 + 48 + 12 = 78 m. 108 m treats the whole 9 s as if the speed were 12 m/s throughout, and 66 m leaves out the slowing-down triangle.

stem: A velocity-time graph shows a body speeding up uniformly from rest to 10 m/s in 4 s and then slowing uniformly to rest in the next 6 s. Its average speed over the 10 s is
explanation: Total distance = area of the triangle = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 m, so average speed = 50/10 = 5 m/s. 50 m/s confuses the distance with the speed, and 10 m/s is the maximum speed, not the average.

stem: The velocity-time graph of a scooter is a straight line falling from 30 m/s at t = 0 to zero at t = 6 s. The magnitude of its deceleration is
explanation: Deceleration = magnitude of slope = 30/6 = 5 m/s². 90 is the area under the graph (the stopping distance in metres), and 0.2 inverts the slope (6/30).

stem: The velocity-time graph of a particle is a straight line from +20 m/s at t = 0 to −20 m/s at t = 4 s. Over these 4 s, the particle's displacement and the distance it covers are respectively
explanation: The line crosses the axis at t = 2 s. The area above the axis is ½ × 2 × 20 = +20 m and the area below is −20 m, so displacement = 0 while distance = 20 + 20 = 40 m. Adding the two areas as positive gives distance, not displacement.

stem: The displacement-time graph of a body is a straight line passing through the origin and inclined to the time axis. This shows that the body
explanation: The slope of a displacement-time graph is velocity; a straight line has a constant slope, so the velocity is constant. Uniform acceleration would make the displacement-time graph a curve (a parabola).

stem: On a velocity-time graph, a curve whose slope keeps increasing with time shows a body with
explanation: The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration, so a steadily steepening curve means the acceleration itself is increasing. Constant acceleration would give a straight line of fixed slope.

stem: A velocity-time graph shows a car moving at a constant 8 m/s from t = 0 to t = 4 s, then slowing uniformly to rest at t = 8 s. Its average velocity over the 8 s is
explanation: Displacement = 8 × 4 + ½ × 4 × 8 = 32 + 16 = 48 m, so average velocity = 48/8 = 6 m/s. 4 m/s is the mean of the start and end velocities, which is valid only for uniform acceleration throughout, and 48 is the displacement in metres.

stem: A body starts from rest. Its acceleration-time graph is a horizontal line at 3 m/s² from t = 0 to t = 4 s. Its velocity at t = 4 s is
explanation: The area under an acceleration-time graph gives the change in velocity: 3 × 4 = 12 m/s, and since it starts from rest, v = 12 m/s. 7 m/s wrongly adds 3 and 4, and 0.75 m/s divides instead of multiplying.

stem: The velocity-time graph of a bus is a straight line rising from 4 m/s at t = 0 to 16 m/s at t = 6 s. The distance covered by the bus in these 6 s is
explanation: The area under the line is a trapezium: ½ × (4 + 16) × 6 = 60 m. 36 m counts only the triangle ½ × 6 × 12 and leaves out the rectangle 4 × 6 due to the initial velocity, and 96 m uses 16 m/s for the whole time.

stem: The velocity-time graph of a ball thrown upward is a straight line sloping downward that crosses the time axis. At the instant the line crosses the axis,
options: velocity is zero but acceleration is not zero
velocity and acceleration are both zero
acceleration is zero and speed is maximum
the ball is back at its starting point
explanation: At the crossing the velocity is zero (the highest point), but the slope of the line, the acceleration g, is the same non-zero value as everywhere else. Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration: the ball is still being pulled down.

stem: Cars A and B leave the same point at the same instant along a straight road. On a velocity-time graph, A is a horizontal line at 10 m/s, while B is a straight line rising from 0 at t = 0 and reaching 10 m/s at t = 5 s. At t = 5 s, where the two lines cross,
options: A and B are side by side
B is 25 m ahead of A
A is 25 m ahead of B
explanation: By t = 5 s, A has covered 10 × 5 = 50 m and B has covered ½ × 5 × 10 = 25 m, so A is 25 m ahead. Crossing lines on a velocity-time graph mean equal velocities, not equal positions; at this moment the gap is largest.

stem: Newton's first law of motion is also known as the law of
explanation: The first law says a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts, which describes inertia. Action and reaction is the third law.

stem: A net force of 20 N acts on a body of mass 4 kg. The acceleration produced is
explanation: From F = ma, a = F/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s². 80 m/s² multiplies instead of dividing, and 0.2 m/s² divides the wrong way round (m/F).

stem: The mass of a body is a measure of its
explanation: Mass measures how strongly a body resists a change in its state of motion, that is, its inertia. Weight is the gravitational force mg, which changes from place to place while mass does not.

stem: Sana, of mass 60 kg, stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is accelerating upward at 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the scale reads
explanation: For upward acceleration, R − mg = ma, so R = m(g + a) = 60 × 12 = 720 N. 480 N is m(g − a), which applies to downward acceleration, and 600 N is her weight when the lift is at rest or moving uniformly.

stem: A person stands on a weighing scale in a lift. The cable breaks and the lift falls freely. While it falls freely, the scale reads
explanation: In free fall a = g downward, so R = m(g − a) = m(g − g) = 0: the person feels weightless. The true weight mg still acts, but the scale no longer pushes on the person, so it reads zero.

stem: Blocks of mass 2 kg and 3 kg are in contact on a smooth horizontal floor. A horizontal force of 10 N pushes the 2 kg block, which pushes the 3 kg block. The force exerted by the 2 kg block on the 3 kg block is
explanation: Both move together with a = 10/(2 + 3) = 2 m/s². The only horizontal force on the 3 kg block is the contact force, so it equals 3 × 2 = 6 N. 4 N is the net force on the 2 kg block (10 − 6), not the contact force.

stem: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang on either side of a light string passing over a smooth, light pulley. Taking g = 10 m/s², the magnitude of their acceleration is
explanation: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (3 − 2) × 10/5 = 2 m/s². Dividing the unbalanced weight of 10 N by only one of the masses (3 kg or 2 kg) gives 10/3 or 5 m/s², but the force must accelerate both masses together.

stem: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang vertically on either side of a light inextensible string over a smooth, light, fixed pulley and are released. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string is
explanation: a = (3 − 2) × 10/5 = 2 m/s². For the 2 kg mass rising, T − 20 = 2 × 2, so T = 24 N (check: 30 − T = 3 × 2 also gives 24 N). 20 N and 30 N are the two weights; the tension lies between them because the masses accelerate.

stem: A block slides down a smooth (frictionless) plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its acceleration is
explanation: Only the component of weight along the slope, mg sin θ, accelerates the block, so a = g sin 30° = 10 × ½ = 5 m/s². 5√3 m/s² wrongly uses cos 30°, which belongs to the component perpendicular to the slope.

stem: A book rests on a table. According to Newton's third law, the reaction to the weight of the book (the pull of the Earth on the book) is
options: the normal force of the table on the book
the force of the book on the table
the pull of the book on the Earth
explanation: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies and are of the same type: the Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls the Earth with an equal and opposite gravitational force. The table's normal force balances the weight, but it acts on the same body (the book) and is a different type of force, so it is not the reaction.

stem: When a stationary bus suddenly starts moving, the standing passengers tend to fall backward. This is due to
explanation: The bus floor moves forward but the upper body of a passenger tends to stay at rest, so it is left behind: this is inertia of rest. Inertia of motion explains falling forward when a moving bus stops suddenly.

stem: A body has a mass of 6 kg on the Earth. On the Moon, where the acceleration due to gravity is one-sixth of that on the Earth, its mass is
explanation: Mass is the quantity of matter and does not depend on location, so it stays 6 kg. Only the weight mg becomes one-sixth on the Moon; 1 kg wrongly scales the mass as if it were weight.

stem: A constant net force of 12 N acts on a 3 kg body initially at rest. The distance moved by the body in the first 5 s is
explanation: a = F/m = 12/3 = 4 m/s², so s = ½at² = ½ × 4 × 25 = 50 m. 100 m forgets the ½, and 20 m is the velocity after 5 s (at = 20 m/s), not the distance.

stem: A 5 kg box is pulled along a horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 30 N. The friction force on the box is 10 N. The acceleration of the box is
explanation: Net force = 30 − 10 = 20 N, so a = 20/5 = 4 m/s². 6 m/s² ignores friction (30/5), and 8 m/s² wrongly adds friction to the pull.

stem: A 4 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is tied to a light string that passes over a smooth pulley at the table edge and carries a 1 kg mass hanging freely. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string while the system moves is
explanation: The weight of the hanging mass (10 N) accelerates both masses: a = 10/(4 + 1) = 2 m/s². The only horizontal force on the 4 kg block is the tension, so T = 4 × 2 = 8 N. 10 N would be the tension only if the system were at rest; the falling mass needs T < mg.

stem: Zainab, of mass 50 kg, stands on a weighing scale in a lift moving downward with a constant velocity of 3 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the scale reads
explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero and R = mg = 50 × 10 = 500 N. The scale reading changes only when the lift accelerates; the value of the velocity itself does not matter.

stem: A rope can bear a maximum tension of 360 N. It is used to lift a 30 kg load vertically. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum upward acceleration the load can be given without breaking the rope is
explanation: T − mg = ma gives 360 − 300 = 30a, so a = 2 m/s². 12 m/s² divides the whole tension by the mass and ignores that 300 N of it is needed just to support the weight.

stem: A net force acting on a body of constant mass always produces
options: a constant velocity in its own direction
a motion directly opposite to the force
no change in the body's momentum
explanation: By Newton's second law, F = ma, so a net force produces an acceleration in the direction of the force. A constant velocity is what happens when the net force is zero.

stem: The momentum of a 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s is
explanation: Momentum p = mv = 2 × 5 = 10 kg m s⁻¹. 25 is the kinetic energy ½mv² in joules, a different quantity.

stem: The SI unit of impulse is
explanation: Impulse = force × time, so its unit is N s (equivalent to kg m s⁻¹, the unit of momentum). N m is the unit of work or torque, and kg m s⁻² is the newton itself.

stem: The impulse of a force acting on a body is equal to the
options: rate of change of its momentum
explanation: Impulse = FΔt = Δp, the change in momentum. The rate of change of momentum is the force itself, and force × distance is work.

stem: A force of 50 N acts on a body for 0.2 s. The change in the momentum of the body is
explanation: Change in momentum = impulse = FΔt = 50 × 0.2 = 10 N s. 250 N s divides 50 by 0.2 instead of multiplying.

stem: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at right angles at 10 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 10 m/s. The magnitude of the change in its momentum is
explanation: Taking the rebound direction as positive, Δp = 0.2 × 10 − 0.2 × (−10) = 4 kg m s⁻¹. Zero comes from ignoring that velocity reverses direction; momentum is a vector, so the change is double the initial momentum.

stem: A cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg moving at 20 m/s is hit straight back along its path at 30 m/s. The bat is in contact with the ball for 0.01 s. The average force exerted by the bat on the ball is
explanation: Because the velocity reverses, Δp = 0.15 × (30 + 20) = 7.5 kg m s⁻¹, and F = Δp/Δt = 7.5/0.01 = 750 N. 150 N subtracts the speeds (30 − 20), forgetting that the direction has changed.

stem: A fielder pulls his hands backward while catching a fast cricket ball. He does this
options: to reduce the total change in the ball's momentum
to increase stopping time, lowering force
to increase the impulse given to the ball
to increase the momentum of the ball
explanation: The change in momentum of the ball (from mv to zero) is fixed, so the impulse FΔt is fixed. Increasing the stopping time Δt reduces the average force on the hands. The change in momentum itself is not reduced by moving the hands.

stem: A force acts on a 0.5 kg body initially at rest. The force rises uniformly from 0 to 40 N in 0.1 s and then falls uniformly back to 0 in a further 0.1 s. The speed of the body afterwards is
explanation: Impulse = area under the force-time graph = ½ × 0.2 × 40 = 4 N s, which equals the change in momentum, so v = 4/0.5 = 8 m/s. 16 m/s forgets the ½ in the triangle's area, and 4 m/s mistakes the impulse for the speed.

stem: A body of mass 2 kg has a kinetic energy of 100 J. The magnitude of its momentum is
explanation: p = √(2mK) = √(2 × 2 × 100) = √400 = 20 kg m s⁻¹ (equivalently v = 10 m/s and p = 2 × 10). 10 kg m s⁻¹ confuses the speed with the momentum, and 400 forgets the square root.

stem: Two bodies of masses 1 kg and 4 kg have equal momenta. The ratio of their kinetic energies (1 kg body : 4 kg body) is
explanation: K = p²/2m, so with equal p, kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass: K₁ : K₂ = 4 : 1. 1 : 4 assumes K is directly proportional to mass, which holds only for equal speeds.

stem: The rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to
explanation: Newton's second law in its general form is F = Δp/Δt: the net force equals the rate of change of momentum. The impulse equals the change in momentum, not its rate of change.

stem: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest by its brakes in 5 s. The average braking force is
explanation: F = Δp/Δt = (1000 × 20)/5 = 4000 N. 100 000 N multiplies the momentum by the time instead of dividing.

stem: The momentum of a 2 kg body moving in a straight line increases from 6 kg m s⁻¹ to 14 kg m s⁻¹ without changing direction. The increase in its kinetic energy is
explanation: K = p²/2m, so ΔK = (14² − 6²)/(2 × 2) = (196 − 36)/4 = 40 J (speeds 3 m/s and 7 m/s give 9 J and 49 J). 16 J wrongly squares the change in momentum, (8²)/4, instead of taking the difference of the squares.

stem: A machine gun fires 10 bullets per second, each of mass 50 g, with a speed of 400 m/s. The average force needed to hold the gun in place is
explanation: Force = momentum given to bullets per second = 10 × 0.05 × 400 = 200 N. 20 N is the momentum of a single bullet, and 200 000 N comes from using 50 g as 50 kg.

stem: The total momentum of a system of bodies remains constant when
options: the colliding bodies are at rest
explanation: Momentum is conserved for an isolated system, one on which the net external force is zero. Kinetic energy need not be conserved; momentum is conserved in inelastic collisions too.

stem: A 4 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet with a muzzle speed of 400 m/s. The recoil speed of the rifle is
explanation: Initial momentum is zero, so 4V = 0.02 × 400 = 8 kg m s⁻¹, giving V = 2 m/s backward. 8 m/s is the bullet's momentum value, not the rifle's speed.

stem: A 3 kg object at rest explodes into two pieces of 1 kg and 2 kg. The 1 kg piece moves off at 10 m/s. The velocity of the 2 kg piece is
options: 5 m/s, opposite to the 1 kg piece
5 m/s, same way as the 1 kg piece
10 m/s, opposite to the 1 kg piece
20 m/s, opposite to the 1 kg piece
explanation: Total momentum stays zero: 1 × 10 + 2v = 0, so v = −5 m/s, that is 5 m/s opposite to the 1 kg piece. The pieces cannot move the same way, or the total momentum would no longer be zero.

stem: A 60 kg man jumps horizontally off the end of a 120 kg boat that was at rest on still water. If he leaves the boat at 4 m/s, the boat moves off in the opposite direction at
explanation: Total momentum is zero before and after: 60 × 4 = 120V, so V = 2 m/s. 8 m/s swaps the masses (120 × 4/60); the heavier boat must move more slowly than the man.

stem: A 4 kg trolley moves at 5 m/s along a smooth horizontal track. A 1 kg bag of sand is dropped vertically onto it and stays on it. The new speed of the trolley is
explanation: The sand has no horizontal momentum, so horizontal momentum is conserved: 4 × 5 = (4 + 1)v, giving v = 4 m/s. The speed cannot stay 5 m/s because the same momentum is now shared by a larger mass.

stem: A 10 g bullet moving horizontally at 500 m/s embeds itself in a 990 g wooden block resting on a smooth horizontal surface. The block and bullet move off together at
explanation: 0.01 × 500 = (0.01 + 0.99)v, so v = 5/1 = 5 m/s. 5.05 m/s divides the momentum by the block's mass alone, forgetting that the bullet moves with the block.

stem: The backward kick (recoil) of a gun when it fires a bullet is explained by
explanation: Before firing the total momentum of gun and bullet is zero; the bullet gains forward momentum, so the gun must gain an equal backward momentum. Energy is also conserved, but it does not fix the direction and size of the recoil velocity.

stem: A shell moving horizontally at 20 m/s explodes into two equal halves. Just after the explosion one half is at rest. The other half moves at
explanation: Momentum is conserved: m × 20 = (m/2) × 0 + (m/2)v, so v = 40 m/s in the original direction. 20 m/s would keep the momentum only if the moving half had the full mass.

stem: A 50 kg boy running at 4 m/s jumps onto a 150 kg cart moving at 2 m/s in the same direction on a smooth road. The common speed of the boy and cart is
explanation: 50 × 4 + 150 × 2 = 200v, so v = 500/200 = 2.5 m/s. 3 m/s is the simple mean of the two speeds, which ignores the different masses, and 0.5 m/s results from taking the motions as opposite.

stem: A 60 kg man stands at one end of a 140 kg boat floating at rest on still water. He walks 5 m to the other end of the boat. Ignoring water resistance, the distance the boat moves backward relative to the water is
explanation: The centre of mass of man and boat stays fixed. If the man moves x forward and the boat moves 5 − x back, 60x = 140(5 − x), so x = 3.5 m and the boat moves 1.5 m. 3.5 m is the man's own movement relative to the water, and 15/7 m treats 5 m as the man's ground displacement.

stem: Two balls collide on a smooth horizontal table with no external horizontal force acting. Which quantity is always conserved in the collision?
explanation: With no external force the total momentum of the system is conserved in every collision. Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions, and the momentum of each ball separately changes.

stem: An 80 kg astronaut at rest in space throws a 2 kg tool away from herself at 6 m/s. She moves in the opposite direction at
explanation: Momentum is conserved: 80V = 2 × 6 = 12, so V = 12/80 = 0.15 m/s. 1.5 m/s and 0.015 m/s are decimal-place slips.

stem: In a perfectly elastic collision, the total kinetic energy is
explanation: An elastic collision is defined as one in which kinetic energy is conserved, and momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system. Losing kinetic energy while conserving momentum describes an inelastic collision.

stem: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the colliding bodies
options: both come to rest in all cases
explanation: A perfectly inelastic collision is one where the bodies move together with a common velocity afterwards, so the maximum kinetic energy is lost. They come to rest only if the total momentum was zero.

stem: A ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with an identical ball at rest. After the collision, the velocities of the first and second balls are respectively
explanation: For equal masses in a one-dimensional elastic collision the balls exchange velocities, so the first stops and the second moves off at 6 m/s. 3 m/s each conserves momentum but loses half the kinetic energy, so it cannot be elastic.

stem: A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m/s collides with a 4 kg trolley at rest and they stick together. Their common velocity is
explanation: 2 × 6 = (2 + 4)v, so v = 12/6 = 2 m/s. 3 m/s divides the speed by 2 as if the masses were equal.

stem: A 3 kg ball moving at 4 m/s collides with a 1 kg ball at rest and they stick together. The kinetic energy lost in the collision is
explanation: Common velocity v = (3 × 4)/4 = 3 m/s. KE before = ½ × 3 × 16 = 24 J and KE after = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J, so 6 J is lost. 18 J is the kinetic energy remaining, not the loss, and zero would apply only to an elastic collision.

stem: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a 1 kg ball at rest. The velocity of the 1 kg ball after the collision is
explanation: For an elastic collision with the target at rest, v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂) = 2 × 2 × 6/3 = 8 m/s (and v₁ = (2 − 1) × 6/3 = 2 m/s; momentum 12 = 2 × 2 + 1 × 8). 12 m/s (2u) is the limit only when the moving ball is very much heavier than the target.

stem: A 1 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a 2 kg ball at rest. Immediately after the collision, the 1 kg ball moves at
explanation: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂) = (1 − 2) × 6/3 = −2 m/s, so it rebounds at 2 m/s; the 2 kg ball moves at 2 × 1 × 6/3 = 4 m/s. Zero would be correct only for equal masses; a lighter ball hitting a heavier one bounces back.

stem: A tennis ball hits a massive rigid wall head-on at 15 m/s in a perfectly elastic collision. It rebounds with a speed of
explanation: In an elastic collision with a very massive body, the light ball's velocity simply reverses, so it rebounds at 15 m/s and its kinetic energy is unchanged. 30 m/s confuses the change in velocity with the final speed.

stem: In a one-dimensional elastic collision between two bodies, the relative velocity of separation after the collision is
explanation: Combining conservation of momentum and kinetic energy gives u₁ − u₂ = v₂ − v₁: the speed of separation equals the speed of approach. Zero relative velocity after collision describes a perfectly inelastic collision.

stem: A 2 kg ball moving east at 5 m/s collides head-on with a 3 kg ball moving west at 5 m/s, and they stick together. Their common velocity is
explanation: Taking east as positive, 2 × 5 + 3 × (−5) = 5v, so v = −5/5 = −1 m/s, which is 1 m/s west. Treating both velocities as positive would give 5 m/s, ignoring that momentum is a vector.

stem: Which of the following collisions is closest to perfectly elastic?
options: Clay hitting and sticking to a floor
Two cars crumpling in a crash
A bullet lodging in a wooden block
explanation: Collisions between gas molecules lose essentially no kinetic energy, so they are treated as elastic. Clay, crashing cars and a lodged bullet all lose kinetic energy to heat, sound and deformation.

stem: Two identical balls move towards each other along a straight line, the first at 4 m/s and the second at 2 m/s, and collide elastically head-on. Taking the first ball's initial direction as positive, their velocities after the collision (first, second) are
explanation: Equal masses in a one-dimensional elastic collision exchange velocities: the first takes −2 m/s and the second takes +4 m/s. 1 m/s each is the common velocity if they stuck together, which would lose kinetic energy.

stem: A 4 kg ball moving at 3 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a 2 kg ball at rest. The fraction of the initial kinetic energy transferred to the 2 kg ball is
explanation: v₂ = 2 × 4 × 3/6 = 4 m/s, so the 2 kg ball gains ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J out of ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J, a fraction 16/18 = 8/9. 1/9 is the fraction kept by the 4 kg ball (it moves on at 1 m/s with 2 J).

stem: In an inelastic collision, the kinetic energy that is lost is mainly converted into
options: an increase in the bodies' mass
explanation: The lost kinetic energy goes into heating, sound and permanent change of shape of the bodies. Momentum is not a form of energy, and it is conserved anyway.

stem: Water leaves a hose at 5 m/s at a rate of 2 kg/s and strikes a wall at right angles. The water does not rebound. The force exerted by the water on the wall is
explanation: F = (mass per second) × change in velocity = 2 × 5 = 10 N. 20 N would apply only if the water bounced back at 5 m/s, doubling the change in velocity.

stem: Water flows out of a pipe of cross-sectional area 0.01 m² at 4 m/s and strikes a wall at right angles without rebounding. Taking the density of water as 1000 kg/m³, the force on the wall is
explanation: Mass per second = ρAv = 1000 × 0.01 × 4 = 40 kg/s, and F = (mass per second) × v = 40 × 4 = ρAv² = 160 N. 40 N stops at the mass flow rate and forgets to multiply by the change in velocity, while 320 N assumes the water rebounds.

stem: A horizontal stream of water strikes a wall at right angles and comes to rest without splashing back. The force exerted on the wall equals
explanation: Force = rate of change of momentum = (mass striking per second) × (change in velocity) = (Δm/Δt) × v. Mass × speed is momentum, not force; it must be divided by time, which is what the mass flow rate does.

stem: Water flows from a pipe of fixed cross-section and strikes a wall at right angles without rebounding. If the speed of the water is doubled, the force on the wall
explanation: F = ρAv²: doubling v doubles both the mass arriving per second (ρAv) and the change in velocity of each kilogram, so F becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times. Choosing doubles counts only one of these two effects.

stem: Water leaves the nozzle of a fire hose at 20 m/s at a rate of 3 kg/s. The backward force that the firefighter must apply to hold the nozzle steady is
explanation: The nozzle gives momentum to the water at a rate of (3 kg/s) × (20 m/s) = 60 N, so by the third law the water pushes back on the hose with 60 N. 6.7 N divides the speed by the flow rate instead of multiplying.

stem: A water jet delivers 0.5 kg of water per second at 8 m/s onto a flat plate held at right angles to it. The water bounces straight back at 2 m/s. The force exerted by the jet on the plate is
explanation: Each kilogram changes velocity from +8 m/s to −2 m/s, a change of 10 m/s, so F = 0.5 × 10 = 5 N. 3 N subtracts the speeds (8 − 2), forgetting that the direction reverses, and 4 N ignores the rebound.

stem: The propulsion of a rocket is based on the principle of
explanation: The rocket pushes exhaust gases backward and gains equal forward momentum, so the total momentum of rocket plus gases is conserved. Gravitation acts on the rocket but does not propel it.

stem: A rocket can accelerate in outer space, where there is no air, because
options: the air outside pushes on its exhaust
there is no gravity in outer space
its mass keeps increasing as it moves
explanation: The rocket exerts a backward force on the gases it ejects, and by the third law the gases exert an equal forward force on the rocket. No outside air is needed; the rocket actually works better without air resistance.

stem: A rocket engine ejects 50 kg of exhaust gas per second at a speed of 2000 m/s relative to the rocket. The thrust on the rocket is
explanation: Thrust = (Δm/Δt) × v = 50 × 2000 = 100 000 N = 1 × 10⁵ N. 40 N divides the speed by the mass rate instead of multiplying.

stem: A rocket of mass 5000 kg stands vertically on its launch pad. Its engines produce a thrust of 1.0 × 10⁵ N. Taking g = 10 m/s², its initial upward acceleration is
explanation: Net upward force = thrust − weight = 100 000 − 50 000 = 50 000 N, so a = 50 000/5000 = 10 m/s². 20 m/s² ignores the rocket's weight, which must be overcome before it can accelerate upward.

stem: A rocket in deep space fires its engine with a constant thrust. As its fuel is used up, its acceleration
explanation: a = thrust/mass; with constant thrust and a mass that falls as fuel is ejected, the acceleration keeps increasing. A constant acceleration would need the mass to stay constant.

stem: A 2000 kg rocket ejects exhaust gas at 1000 m/s relative to itself. Taking g = 10 m/s², the minimum rate at which it must eject gas to just lift off vertically is
explanation: To just lift off, thrust must equal weight: (Δm/Δt) × 1000 = 2000 × 10, so Δm/Δt = 20 kg/s. 2 kg/s forgets to multiply the mass by g to get the weight.

stem: A ball is thrown at an angle above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, at the highest point of its path
explanation: At the top the vertical component of velocity is zero but the horizontal component is unchanged, so the velocity is horizontal. The acceleration is still g vertically downward throughout the flight.

stem: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal component of the velocity of a projectile
explanation: Gravity acts only vertically, so there is no horizontal force and the horizontal velocity u cos θ stays constant. It is the vertical component that becomes zero at the top.

stem: For a fixed speed of projection on level ground and no air resistance, the horizontal range of a projectile is greatest when the angle of projection is
explanation: R = u² sin 2θ/g is largest when sin 2θ = 1, that is 2θ = 90° and θ = 45°. At 90° the range is zero because the projectile goes straight up and down.

stem: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its time of flight is
explanation: T = 2u sin θ/g = 2 × 20 × ½/10 = 2 s. 4 s forgets sin θ (it is the flight time for a vertical throw), and 2√3 s wrongly uses cos 30°.

stem: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum height it reaches is
explanation: H = u² sin²θ/2g = 400 × ¼/20 = 5 m. 10 m forgets to square sin θ, and 15 m uses cos²30° instead of sin²30°.

stem: A stone is projected from level ground at 40 m/s at 15° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its horizontal range is
explanation: R = u² sin 2θ/g = 1600 × sin 30°/10 = 1600 × ½/10 = 80 m. 160 m is the maximum range u²/g at 45°, and 80√3 m uses sin 60° by doubling the angle twice.

stem: Two stones are projected from level ground with the same speed, one at 30° and the other at 60° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, the ratio of their horizontal ranges is
explanation: R ∝ sin 2θ, and sin 60° = sin 120°, so complementary angles of projection give equal ranges: 1 : 1. The 60° stone goes higher and stays up longer, but moves more slowly horizontally.

stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a cliff 20 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s², it lands at a horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff of
explanation: Vertical motion: 20 = ½ × 10 × t², so t = 2 s; horizontal distance = 15 × 2 = 30 m. 60 m comes from using t = 4 s (20 = 5t wrongly), and 20 m mistakes the height for the range.

stem: From the same height, Ayesha drops one ball and at the same instant throws an identical ball horizontally. Ignoring air resistance,
options: both land at the same time
explanation: Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g, so they take the same time to fall; the horizontal velocity does not affect the vertical motion. Mass does not affect free-fall time either.

stem: A ball is thrown horizontally at 30 m/s from the top of a tower 80 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s², its speed just before it hits the ground is
explanation: Fall time t = √(2 × 80/10) = 4 s, so vertical velocity = 40 m/s and speed = √(30² + 40²) = 50 m/s. 70 m/s adds the components as numbers instead of as perpendicular vectors.

stem: A projectile is launched from level ground so that its horizontal range equals its maximum height. The angle of projection θ satisfies
explanation: Setting u² sin²θ/2g = 2u² sin θ cos θ/g gives sin θ/2 = 2 cos θ, so tan θ = 4 (about 76°). tan θ = 1 (45°) gives the maximum range, where the range is four times the height.

stem: Ignoring air resistance, the speed of a projectile at its highest point is half its speed of projection. The angle of projection above the horizontal is
explanation: At the top only the horizontal component remains, so u cos θ = u/2, cos θ = ½ and θ = 60°. 30° would give a speed at the top of (√3/2)u, not u/2.

stem: A ball is projected from level ground at 20√2 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum height it reaches is
explanation: Vertical component = 20√2 × (1/√2) = 20 m/s, so H = 20²/(2 × 10) = 20 m. 80 m is the range (u²/g = 800/10), and 40 m forgets the factor 2 in 2g.

stem: Hamza can throw a ball to a maximum horizontal range of 90 m on level ground. Ignoring air resistance, the greatest height he can throw the same ball vertically upward with the same speed is
explanation: Maximum range R = u²/g = 90 m. Thrown straight up, H = u²/2g = 90/2 = 45 m. 22.5 m is the height reached at 45°, u² sin²45°/2g, not in a vertical throw.

stem: A ball is projected at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, its speed 1 s after projection is
explanation: Components: uₓ = 20 cos 30° = 10√3 m/s and u_y = 10 m/s. After 1 s, v_y = 10 − 10 × 1 = 0, so the ball is at its highest point and the speed is just 10√3 m/s. Zero forgets the horizontal component, which never changes.

stem: Ball A is dropped from rest from the top of a 45 m tower. At the same instant ball B is thrown vertically upward at 30 m/s from the ground directly below. Ignoring air resistance, the balls meet after
explanation: Both balls have the same acceleration g, so relative to each other they move uniformly: B approaches A at 30 m/s across a 45 m gap, giving t = 45/30 = 1.5 s. (Check: A falls 5 × 2.25 = 11.25 m and B rises 45 − 11.25 = 33.75 m.) 3 s is the time B would take to reach its own highest point.

stem: A ball thrown horizontally from a height h lands a horizontal distance d from the foot of the building. If the throwing speed is doubled and the height is made 4h, the ball lands at a horizontal distance of
explanation: Fall time t = √(2h/g), so making the height 4h doubles t. Range = ut, and both u and t double, giving 4d. 2d accounts only for the doubled speed and forgets the longer fall time.

stem: According to Newton's third law, an action force and its reaction force
explanation: Action and reaction are equal and opposite but act on two different bodies, so they never cancel each other. Forces that cancel must act on the same body, as in a balanced pair.

stem: A car's speed increases uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s while it travels 100 m. Its acceleration is
explanation: vf² = vi² + 2as gives 900 = 100 + 200a, so a = 800/200 = 4 m/s². 8 m/s² forgets the 2 in 2as, and 0.2 m/s² divides the change in speed by the distance.

stem: The position of a particle moving along a straight line is x = 6t − t², where x is in metres and t in seconds. The particle comes momentarily to rest at
explanation: v = dx/dt = 6 − 2t, which is zero at t = 3 s. At t = 6 s the particle is back at x = 0, which is a return to the start, not the instant of rest.

stem: The position of a particle moving along a straight line is x = 6t − t², where x is in metres and t in seconds. The distance it covers in the first 4 s is
explanation: It moves forward until t = 3 s, reaching x = 9 m, then turns back: x(4) = 24 − 16 = 8 m. Distance = 9 + (9 − 8) = 10 m. 8 m is the displacement, which ignores the reversal of direction.

stem: The unit kg m s⁻¹ is equivalent to
explanation: N s = (kg m s⁻²) × s = kg m s⁻¹, which is why impulse and momentum share a unit. The newton itself is kg m s⁻², and N m is the joule.

stem: The momentum of a body increases from 20 kg m s⁻¹ to 50 kg m s⁻¹ in 3 s along a straight line. The average net force on the body is
explanation: F = Δp/Δt = (50 − 20)/3 = 10 N. 30 N is the change in momentum, not the force, and 70/3 N adds the momenta instead of subtracting.

stem: A 2 kg block is pulled up a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal by a force of 20 N acting parallel to the plane. Taking g = 10 m/s², its acceleration up the plane is
explanation: The weight component down the slope is mg sin 30° = 2 × 10 × ½ = 10 N, so net force = 20 − 10 = 10 N and a = 10/2 = 5 m/s². 10 m/s² ignores the weight component, and 15 m/s² adds it.

stem: A lift carrying Bilal, of mass 70 kg, is moving upward but slowing down at 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the force exerted by the floor on Bilal is
explanation: Slowing while moving up means the acceleration is 2 m/s² downward, so mg − R = ma and R = 70 × (10 − 2) = 560 N. 840 N uses m(g + a), which is wrong because the direction of acceleration, not of motion, decides the sign.

stem: A 0.5 kg ball strikes the floor vertically at 6 m/s and rebounds vertically at 4 m/s. The magnitude of the impulse given to the ball by the floor is
explanation: Taking upward as positive, Δp = 0.5 × 4 − 0.5 × (−6) = 2 + 3 = 5 N s. 1 N s subtracts the speeds (6 − 4), which ignores the reversal of direction.

stem: A 5 kg gun fires a 50 g bullet. The ratio of the kinetic energy of the bullet to the kinetic energy of the recoiling gun is
explanation: Bullet and gun receive equal and opposite momenta, and K = p²/2m, so the ratio K(bullet)/K(gun) = M/m = 5/0.05 = 100. 1/100 inverts the ratio; the lighter body carries most of the kinetic energy.

stem: The forward force exerted on a rocket by the gases it ejects backward is called
explanation: Thrust is the reaction force of the expelled gases on the rocket, equal to the rate at which momentum is given to the gases. Drag is air resistance, which opposes the motion.

stem: A ball is projected at 45° above the horizontal with kinetic energy K. Ignoring air resistance, its kinetic energy at the highest point is
explanation: At the top only the horizontal component u cos 45° = u/√2 remains, so the kinetic energy is ½m(u²/2) = K/2. K/√2 forgets that kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed.

stem: A velocity-time graph is a straight line that starts at the origin and slopes upward with a constant slope. It shows a body moving with
explanation: Starting at the origin means the body starts from rest, and a constant positive slope means a constant acceleration. Uniform velocity would show as a horizontal line.

stem: For any motion, the distance covered by a body is
options: at least as large as displacement
explanation: Distance is the length of the actual path, and the straight-line displacement is the shortest possible path between the two points, so distance ≥ |displacement|. They are equal only for motion in one direction along a straight line; on a round trip the displacement, not the distance, is zero.

stem: A car covers 150 km in 2.5 hours. Its average speed is
explanation: Average speed = distance/time = 150/2.5 = 60 km/h. 375 km/h multiplies instead of dividing.

stem: A body moving at 12 m/s decelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² until it stops. The distance it covers while stopping is
explanation: 0 = vi² − 2as gives s = 144/(2 × 3) = 24 m. 48 m forgets the factor 2 in 2as, and 4 m is the stopping time in seconds (12/3).

stem: A stone thrown vertically upward returns to the thrower's hand after 4 s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, the speed with which it was thrown is
explanation: The upward journey takes half the total time, 2 s, and the speed falls to zero in that time, so u = gt = 10 × 2 = 20 m/s. 40 m/s wrongly uses the whole 4 s as the time to the top.

stem: In a vacuum near the Earth's surface, a feather and a stone dropped together fall with
explanation: Without air resistance the only force is the weight mg, so a = mg/m = g for every body regardless of mass. The feather falls slowly in air only because of air resistance.

stem: The velocity-time graph of a body is a straight line rising from 5 m/s at t = 0 to 15 m/s at t = 5 s. The acceleration of the body is
explanation: Acceleration = slope = (15 − 5)/5 = 2 m/s². 3 m/s² divides the final velocity by the time and ignores the initial 5 m/s, and 50 is the area under the graph (the distance in metres).

stem: A velocity-time graph shows a rickshaw speeding up uniformly from rest to 10 m/s in 2 s, moving at 10 m/s for the next 6 s and then slowing uniformly to rest in 2 s. The total distance covered is
explanation: Area = ½ × 2 × 10 + 6 × 10 + ½ × 2 × 10 = 10 + 60 + 10 = 80 m. 100 m treats all 10 s as if the speed were 10 m/s, and 60 m counts only the constant-speed part.

stem: Taking g = 10 m/s², the weight of a body of mass 8 kg is
explanation: W = mg = 8 × 10 = 80 N. 8 N confuses mass in kilograms with weight in newtons.

stem: A certain force gives a 3 kg body an acceleration of 4 m/s². The same force acting on a 6 kg body gives it an acceleration of
explanation: F = 3 × 4 = 12 N, so on 6 kg, a = 12/6 = 2 m/s²; for a fixed force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. 8 m/s² wrongly makes acceleration increase with mass.

stem: Fatima, of mass 40 kg, stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating downward at 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the scale reads
explanation: For downward acceleration, mg − R = ma, so R = m(g − a) = 40 × 8 = 320 N. 480 N uses m(g + a), which applies to upward acceleration.

stem: Masses of 5 kg and 3 kg hang vertically on either side of a light string passing over a smooth, light, fixed pulley and are released. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string is
explanation: a = (5 − 3) × 10/8 = 2.5 m/s². For the rising 3 kg mass, T − 30 = 3 × 2.5, so T = 37.5 N. 40 N is simply the mean of the two weights, which is not how the tension is found.

stem: A force of 100 N acts on a ball for 0.05 s. The impulse given to the ball is
explanation: Impulse = FΔt = 100 × 0.05 = 5 N s. 2000 N s divides the force by the time instead of multiplying.

stem: A goalkeeper stops a 0.4 kg football moving at 15 m/s in 0.2 s. The average force exerted on the ball is
explanation: Δp = 0.4 × 15 = 6 kg m s⁻¹, so F = 6/0.2 = 30 N. 60 N would apply if the ball were sent back at 15 m/s, and 1.2 N multiplies the momentum by the time.

stem: The momentum of a body of fixed mass is increased by 20%. Its kinetic energy increases by
explanation: K = p²/2m, so K becomes (1.2)² = 1.44 times its value, an increase of 44%. 40% simply doubles the 20% and ignores the cross term (1.2² = 1 + 0.4 + 0.04).

stem: A 2 kg toy cannon at rest fires a 0.1 kg ball horizontally at 30 m/s. The recoil speed of the cannon is
explanation: Total momentum stays zero: 2V = 0.1 × 30 = 3, so V = 1.5 m/s. 3 m/s is the ball's momentum value in kg m s⁻¹, not the cannon's speed.

stem: Blocks of 1 kg and 3 kg on a smooth floor are pushed apart from rest by a compressed spring between them. Their total kinetic energy afterwards is 24 J. The kinetic energy of the 1 kg block is
explanation: The blocks get equal and opposite momenta, and K = p²/2m, so K is inversely proportional to mass: K(1 kg) : K(3 kg) = 3 : 1. The 1 kg block gets ¾ × 24 = 18 J. 6 J gives the larger share to the heavier block, which is the wrong way round.

stem: In an inelastic collision between two bodies with no external force acting, which statement is correct?
options: Kinetic energy is kept, momentum is not
Both momentum and kinetic energy are kept
Momentum is kept, kinetic energy is not
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is kept
explanation: Total momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system, but in an inelastic collision some kinetic energy turns into heat, sound and deformation. Conservation of both is the definition of an elastic collision.

stem: A 1 kg ball moving at 8 m/s collides with a 3 kg ball at rest, and the two stick together. Their common velocity is
explanation: 1 × 8 = (1 + 3)v, so v = 8/4 = 2 m/s. 8/3 m/s divides the momentum by the 3 kg mass alone, forgetting the 1 kg ball moves with it, and 4 m/s assumes equal masses.

stem: A very heavy ball moving at speed u collides head-on and elastically with a very light ball at rest. Just after the collision, the light ball moves at about
explanation: v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂), which tends to 2u when m₁ is much larger than m₂; the heavy ball carries on at almost u. Speed u for the target is the result for equal masses, not for a very heavy striker.

stem: Water strikes a wall at right angles and stops. If the mass of water striking per second is doubled while its speed stays the same, the force on the wall
explanation: F = (mass per second) × change in velocity; doubling the mass rate at the same speed doubles the force. Four times would need the speed to double as well.

stem: A rocket engine ejects gas at 1500 m/s relative to the rocket and produces a thrust of 3 × 10⁴ N. The mass of gas ejected per second is
explanation: Thrust = (Δm/Δt) × v, so Δm/Δt = 30 000/1500 = 20 kg/s. 0.05 kg/s inverts the division (1500/30 000).

stem: Ignoring air resistance, the acceleration of a projectile throughout its flight is
explanation: The only force on the projectile is its weight, so its acceleration is g vertically downward at every point, including the top. Zero velocity in the vertical direction at the top does not mean zero acceleration.

stem: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its horizontal range is
explanation: R = u² sin 2θ/g = 400 × sin 90°/10 = 40 m. 80 m uses 2u²/g (an extra factor 2), and 10 m is the maximum height u² sin²45°/2g, not the range.

stem: A ball is projected from level ground at 40 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², the horizontal distance it has covered when it reaches its highest point is
explanation: Time to the top = u sin θ/g = 20/10 = 2 s, and horizontal velocity = 40 cos 30° = 20√3 m/s, so the distance = 20√3 × 2 = 40√3 m (half the range). 80√3 m is the full range, reached only when the ball lands.

stem: A body moving with uniform acceleration covers 20 m in the 2nd second and 40 m in the 4th second of its motion. Its initial velocity is
explanation: Distance in the nth second is u + a(2n − 1)/2, so 20 = u + 1.5a and 40 = u + 3.5a. Subtracting gives 2a = 20, a = 10 m/s², and then u = 20 − 15 = 5 m/s. 10 m/s is the acceleration value, not the initial velocity.
